title: Sisters and brothers of America
hookLine: a young monk greets Chicago as family, then says his tradition accepts other paths
carry: accept other paths, not just tolerate them

cards: Chicago. A big hall, a platform crowded with delegates from many religions, each waiting a turn to speak. Among them is a young Hindu monk.
In Ramakrishna's room he was called Narendranath. Here he's Swami Vivekananda, a long way from Bengal.
When his turn finally comes, he stands up, faces the crowd, and opens not with an argument or a defense of his tradition, but with a greeting.

teach.b: The occasion was the World's Parliament of Religions, and his short talk on the opening day is printed in his collected works as the response to the welcome. His first words were: Sisters and Brothers of America.
Tradition says the hall broke into applause before he could go on. Whatever the crowd heard in it, the greeting makes strangers into family before a single idea is offered. Then come the ideas.
He thanks his listeners in the name of the monks of his order and of the Hindu people.
His tradition, he says, taught him not only to tolerate other paths but to accept them. He gives two texts to show what he means.
First, a hymn he says he learned as a boy: as rivers rising in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so the different paths people take, crooked or straight, all lead to you, Lord.
Second, the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says, in effect: whoever comes to me, by whatever road, I reach them.
Then he names what he hopes is ending: sectarianism, bigotry and fanaticism, which, he says, have filled the earth with violence.
He hopes the bell that rang that morning to open the Parliament will turn out to be their death knell. A greeting, two old texts, one hope. He didn't arrive with a new teaching.

He carried in songs and verses from home, and underneath them is a teaching many Hindus grow up with: the paths to God are many, and God receives people on every one of them. Not, you're wrong but I'll put up with you.

how: Vivekananda's Chicago addresses are printed in his Complete Works, and Hindu and Vedanta groups read them aloud in study circles and at gatherings.

games.q: a classmate of another faith asks if you think their path is wrong. which answer comes from Vivekananda's talk?
o: "my tradition teaches me to accept your path, not just tolerate it."
games.why: he said his tradition taught not only tolerance but acceptance, with a hymn of rivers meeting in one sea and the Gita's word that whoever comes, by whatever road, is reached.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose faith or way of life is different from yours: a classmate, a coworker, an in-law, a neighbor. Silently greet them the way he greeted Chicago, as a sister or a brother, without forcing a feeling.

Then picture their road as a river, starting somewhere you've never been, still running toward the sea. Notice if any part of you wants to say only my river counts. If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer you already know.

wordCard.voice: Vivekananda. Ramakrishna's disciple, the monk who greeted a hall in Chicago as sisters and brothers before saying anything else.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the monastic name of the young man once called Narendranath.

carryVoice: Your line: accept other paths, not just tolerate them. Many rivers, one sea. See you tomorrow.
